findings.title: Headline transcripts are in a legacy schema the released evaluator cannot parse
findings.quote:
- We share logs of most of our experiments under `logs`.
- Please note that some logs were generated with our previous code base and the logs were saved in a slightly different scheme. Please refer to `old_code` branch (we will add more details TBD).
findings.claim: 22 of the 25 shipped log bundles (all .zip files, including output_base_best_allcoop_gpt4.zip behind Table 1 row5 / Table 3 GPT-4 / Table 8 temp0 = 81/33/100/1.4, plus all Llama/Mixtral Table-3 logs, Table-2 mixed-population, and most Table-4/6 logs) store rounds as legacy [agent, answer] lists with no config.txt/scores_files; the shipped evaluate_deals.ipynb only loads files whose name startswith('history') and reads round['agent']/round['public_answer'], so it cannot parse them, and the compatible loader is deferred to an unshipped 'old_code' branch.
findings.concern: Most of the paper's headline numbers (Tables 1, 2, 3, and most of 4 and 6) cannot be regenerated from the released transcripts with the released code at the audited commit; only baseextended (Table 4) and temp=1 (Table 8) are in the current schema (and both reproduce).
findings.resolution: Merge the 'old_code' loader into this commit (or convert the legacy answers*.json to the current history schema), and include config.txt + scores_files inside each log bundle so evaluate_deals.ipynb can score them.
findings.reason: README quote confirmed verbatim at lines 206-207; re-ran schema_survey.py against code/S-Abdelnabi__LLM-Deliberation/logs and it classifies exactly 3 of 25 bundles CURRENT (dict/public_answer, incl. baseextended and temp1 dirs) and the other 22 (all .zip, incl. output_base_best_allcoop_gpt4.zip) LEGACY(list[agent,answer]); evaluate_deals.ipynb was inspected directly and only globs files startswith('history') then reads round_['agent']/round_['public_answer']; the cloned repo has no .git (flat snapshot), consistent with 'old_code' branch being unshipped.

findings.title: No code for the rule-based baseline (Table 5), random-deal baseline (§4.7), or ToM best-guess (61%/42%)
findings.quote: We also add a repeated rule-based baseline, shown in Table 5, that is based on simulating randomized interaction without using LLMs.
findings.claim: The repo's only scripts are the simulation driver and 3 evaluation artefacts (evaluate_deals.ipynb, adjust_games.ipynb, score_leakage.py); none implements the Table 5 heuristic algorithm (start from a random deal, improve one option at a time per agent), the §4.7 random-deal-per-round baseline (reported 10%/3%), or the ToM best-guess preference-matching computation (reported 61% GPT-4 / 42% GPT-3.5).
findings.concern: Three reported quantitative comparisons that contextualise the LLM results (the difficulty lower bound in Table 5, the random-chance baseline, and the ToM metric) have no generating code, so those numbers are not independently checkable from the repo.
findings.resolution: Add the scripts that produce Table 5, the §4.7 random-deal baseline, and the ToM best-guess percentages.
findings.reason: Paper quote confirmed verbatim in paper_text.txt; repo-wide find for *.py/*.ipynb (absence claim warrants this) turns up exactly the simulation driver files plus evaluation/{adjust_games.ipynb, evaluate_deals.ipynb, score_leakage.py, eval_utils.py}, and a case-insensitive grep for rule-based/ToM/best-guess/random-deal terms across all .py/.ipynb returns zero hits.

findings.title: Score/threshold sets for the Table 4 difficulty rows (Base 30/4 and 17/2) are not shipped
findings.quote: base game, this ratio is 55/720; for the difficulty levels in Table 4, it would be 30/720 and 17/720
findings.claim: games_descriptions/base ships a single score set (SportCo min=55, ...) whose feasible-deal count is 55/720 (n-1-way), matching the base row; but the two difficulty variants in Table 4 (Base 30/4 and Base 17/2, i.e. 30/720 and 17/720 feasible deals) require different raised thresholds, and no such score set exists in games_descriptions/ (verified by enumerating every shipped score file).
findings.concern: The Table 4 difficulty rows and their reported success numbers cannot be reproduced because the modified thresholds that define those games are not in the repo (and their logs are in the unparsable legacy zips).
findings.resolution: Ship the score_files for the 30/720 and 17/720 difficulty variants (or a script that generates them).
findings.reason: Paper quote confirmed (line 841 of paper_text.txt, modulo an expected ligature artifact in 'difficulty'); games_descriptions/ contains only base, base_7players, base_rewritten, game1, game2, game3 -- no directory or score file for the 30/720 or 17/720 variants; check_feasibility.py independently confirms base's shipped scores give exactly 55/720 (n-1-way), matching the base row and leaving the two difficulty rows unaccounted for.

findings.title: Simulation will not import on Python < 3.12 (PEP 701 nested-quote f-string)
findings.claim: prompt_utils.py lines 9 and 11 use same-quote nesting inside an f-string ({slot['agent']}), which is only valid syntax on Python >= 3.12 (PEP 701); the file fails to byte-compile on Python 3.10.13 with 'SyntaxError: f-string: unmatched '[' ', and main.py imports it via `from rounds import RoundPrompts` -> `from prompt_utils import ...`, so the whole simulation aborts at import.
findings.concern: The README setup (conda install pytorch==2.3.0, transformers, ...) does not pin Python >= 3.12, and pytorch 2.3.0 supports 3.8-3.12; on a default (<3.12) install the simulation half of the artefact cannot run at all (the evaluation notebooks are unaffected).
findings.resolution: Rewrite the nested f-strings with a different inner quote or `.format`, and/or pin Python >= 3.12 in the setup instructions.
findings.reason: Quote matches line 11 exactly; py_compile on the actual verifier Python (3.10.13, matching the claim precisely) reproduces the exact cited SyntaxError at line 9; confirmed the import chain main.py -> `from rounds import RoundPrompts` -> rounds.py `from prompt_utils import format_history, build_first_slot`, so any import of main.py aborts.

findings.title: Non-Azure OpenAI path returns the message object, not its text
findings.claim: In the `'gpt' in model and not self.azure` branch, prompt() returns response.choices[0].message (a message object), whereas the Azure branch (line 69) returns response.choices[0].message.content (a str); the returned value flows to save_utils.extract_answer which does string operations (`'<ANSWER>' in answer`, answer.split(...)), so the non-Azure OpenAI path breaks.
findings.concern: Anyone running with the plain OpenAI API (no --azure) hits a type error at answer parsing; the paper's own runs used Azure (models named 'gpt-4-low'), so results are unaffected, but the advertised OpenAI path is non-functional.
findings.resolution: Return response.choices[0].message.content in the non-Azure branch.
findings.reason: Quote matches line 59 exactly; confirmed the `not self.azure` branch returns response.choices[0].message while the azure branch (a few lines below) returns response.choices[0].message.content; confirmed save_utils.extract_answer does string containment/split on its input ('<ANSWER>' in answer, answer.split(...)), which would TypeError on a message object.

findings.title: load_scores parses the min-threshold line twice (missing break creates a spurious issue)
findings.quote:
for i,line in enumerate(Lines):
    if i == len(Lines) - 1: #min thresholds 
        scores['min'] = line.strip()
    scores[issue_names[i]] = [int(num.strip()) for num in line.split(',')]
findings.claim: On the last line (the minimum threshold) the code sets scores['min'] but does not break/continue, so it also executes scores[issue_names[i]] = [...], parsing the threshold as an extra bogus issue (e.g. 'F' for a 5-issue game); the equivalent loader in eval_utils.py load_setup uses `break`, showing the intended behaviour.
findings.concern: The spurious issue key is a latent defect (and scores['min'] ends up a str here vs int in eval_utils); it has no observed downstream effect because the extra key's placeholders (#F1_NUM etc.) do not appear in the instruction files, but the code does not do what it plainly intends.
findings.resolution: Add `break` (or `continue`) after setting scores['min'], matching eval_utils.py.
findings.reason: Quote matches initial_prompts.py lines 39-42 exactly (whitespace stripped); confirmed no break/continue after scores['min'] is set, so the same line also falls into scores[issue_names[i]]=...; confirmed evaluation/eval_utils.py's load_setup has the equivalent loop with an explicit `break` right after setting scores['min'] (int), showing the intended/diverging behaviour.

findings.title: Shipped game3 scores give 55/35 feasible deals, but Table 4 reports New 3 (57/34)
findings.quote: game3,720,ge(adjust_games),55,35,"{""Federal government of Germany"": 55, ""Private investors"": 63, ""State government of Saarland"": 45, ""Environmental activists"": 50, ""France"": 65, ""Local community of Neunkirchen"": 50}",paper New3: 57/34
findings.claim: Enumerating all 720 game3 deals with the shipped games_descriptions/game3 scores under the adjust_games.ipynb criterion (>=) yields 55 (n-1)-way and 35 n-way feasible deals; the paper's Table 4 reports New 3 as (57/34). game1 (57/21) and game2 (57/18) reproduce exactly under the same procedure, so the game3 score files in the repo differ slightly from the version used for the paper.
findings.concern: The shipped game3 definition does not exactly reproduce its reported feasibility statistics (off by +2/-1); a reader recomputing difficulty gets different numbers.
findings.resolution: Confirm which game3 scores/thresholds were used for Table 4 and update the repo (or the table).
findings.reason: Copied check_feasibility.py to _verifier_code/ and re-ran it read-only against code/S-Abdelnabi__LLM-Deliberation/games_descriptions; output row 12 of the regenerated CSV matches the cited quote exactly (game3, ge(adjust_games), 55, 35) while game1 (57/21) and game2 (57/18) reproduce the paper's numbers exactly, confirming game3 alone is off.

findings.title: Feasibility statistics use '>=' but success metrics use '>' — inconsistent, up to 21-point effect
findings.quote: A deal is feasible if it exceeds the thresholds
findings.claim: The reported feasibility statistics (Table 4 '(55/12)', baseextended 204, New1 57/21, New2 57/18; and the §4.7 random-chance ratios such as 55/720) reproduce only with a non-strict acceptance test — adjust_games.ipynb cell uses `if deal_score >= agents[party]['scores']['min']`. The reported success rates (Final/Any) reproduce only with a strict test — evaluate_deals.ipynb loop_all_parties uses `if party_score > agents[name_i]['scores']['min']` (my strict-'>' replication matched the paper: baseextended 63.8/18.8/96.2, temp=1 68.8/6.2/96.9). So a deal that lands a party exactly on its threshold counts as feasible for the denominator but as non-agreeing for the numerator.
findings.concern: The same tables mix two acceptance criteria; the choice is material — recomputing baseextended success with '>=' (the criterion behind the reported feasible-set sizes and consistent with the agent rule 'cannot accept ... less than min') gives 5/6-way = 85.0 vs the reported 63.8, a 21.2-point swing (and base's feasible count is 55 under '>=' vs 37 under the paper's own 'exceeds' wording). Qualitative conclusions (GPT-4 > others; harder games score lower) are unaffected and the direction of the success metric is conservative, but the exact numbers and the difficulty-vs-success framing are internally inconsistent.
findings.resolution: Use one acceptance criterion consistently for both the feasible-set counts and the success metrics (align both with the paper's 'exceeds' definition, or with the agent instruction '>='), and restate the affected numbers.
findings.reason: Paper quote confirmed verbatim (paper_text.txt line 178-179, 'A deal is feasible if it exceeds the thresholds'); directly inspected both notebooks and confirmed evaluate_deals.ipynb's loop_all_parties uses strict `>` while adjust_games.ipynb's feasibility cells use `>=`, exactly as claimed; re-ran check_feasibility.py and confirmed the two criteria give materially different counts (e.g. base 55/12 under >= vs 37/6 under >), corroborating the core inconsistency. The specific '85.0 vs 63.8' success-rate recomputation is supporting color that goes beyond the cited check_script (it requires re-scoring real logs) and was not independently re-derived within budget, but it does not carry the finding's core, code-verified claim.
